task_row_model.query: Consider the boundary value problem u''(x) + λ u(x) = f(x) on (0,π) with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions u(0)=u(π)=0. Derive an explicit representation of the solution using eigenfunction expansions, state precisely for which λ the differential operator is invertible, give the spectral series expression for the Green's function, and explain what occurs in the resonance case when λ equals an eigenvalue.

documents.content: For a function defined on (0,π) that vanishes at the endpoints one often expands it in a Fourier sine series. The sine basis {sin(nx)}_{n=1}^∞ is orthogonal on (0,π) with ∫_0^π sin(nx) sin(mx) dx = (π/2) δ_{mn}. If f(x) is piecewise smooth or in L^2(0,π) then f(x)=∑_{n=1}^∞ b_n sin(nx) with coefficients b_n=(2/π)∫_0^π f(s) sin(ns) ds. Convergence in L^2 is guaranteed and pointwise convergence holds under additional smoothness; Parseval's identity gives the squared-norm relation between coefficients and function energy.

A standard numerical approach for second-order two-point boundary value problems is to discretize the interval [0,π] with a uniform grid and approximate the second derivative by central differences. This yields a tridiagonal linear system A u = f where A has entries coming from the stencil u_{i-1}-2u_i+u_{i+1} divided by h^2 plus any potential diagonal term from λ. Dirichlet boundary values are incorporated by modifying the right-hand side. The resulting tridiagonal matrix can be solved efficiently with the Thomas algorithm; error estimates follow from truncation of the finite-difference approximation.

On (0,π) with u(0)=u(π)=0 expand f and u in the sine basis sin(nx). With b_n=(2/π)∫_0^π f(s) sin(ns) ds and u(x)=∑_{n≥1} a_n sin(nx), substitution gives (-n^2+λ)a_n=b_n so a_n=b_n/(λ-n^2) provided λ≠n^2 for every n. Thus for non-eigenvalue λ the solution is u(x)=∑_{n=1}^∞ (2/π)(∫_0^π f(s) sin(ns) ds)/(λ-n^2) sin(nx). The associated Green's function admits the spectral expansion G(x,s)=∑_{n=1}^∞ (2/π) sin(nx) sin(ns)/(λ-n^2). If λ equals n0^2 (resonance) a solution exists only if b_{n0}=0 (orthogonality to the eigenmode), and any solution is determined up to adding C sin(n0 x) from the homogeneous nullspace.

One can construct a Green's function for a regular second-order linear ODE by using two linearly independent solutions of the homogeneous equation. Choose φ(x) satisfying the left boundary condition and ψ(x) satisfying the right boundary condition; the Green's function is formed by matching these at the source point s and dividing by the constant Wronskian W(φ,ψ). Explicitly, for x<s use G(x,s)=φ(x)ψ(s)/W and for x>s use G(x,s)=φ(s)ψ(x)/W, ensuring continuity at x=s and a jump of 1 in the first derivative. This procedure yields an integral representation u(x)=∫_0^π G(x,s) f(s) ds.

Orthogonal polynomial systems on intervals are eigenfunctions of certain Sturm–Liouville problems. For example, Legendre polynomials P_n on [-1,1] satisfy ( (1-x^2) P_n' )' + n(n+1) P_n = 0 and are orthogonal with respect to weight 1. Recurrence relations and three-term identities allow efficient computation and spectral properties such as orthogonality and normalization. These polynomial bases are useful for spectral methods on symmetric intervals, but their weight functions and domain differ from sine bases on (0,π), so mapping or change of variables is typically required when applying them to other boundary-value contexts.
